enrichment.short_title: PPG3 brownfield presumption on greenfield housing appeal
key_facts: A developer appealed against refusal of planning permission for a large greenfield residential scheme at Lower Warton in Lancashire.
The inspector recommended permission, but the Secretary of State dismissed the appeal because the site conflicted with PPG3's presumption in favour of previously developed land.
Richards J quashed the decision for inadequate reasons on housing land supply and windfall sites.
On appeal, the Secretary of State accepted redetermination was required but sought to clarify how PPG3 paragraphs 32 and 34 interact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against part of a High Court order remitting a planning appeal for redetermination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal disposed with no further order; matter remitted for redetermination in light of the judgment below as clarified; Secretary of State to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 34 of PPG3 is a relevant factor in development control when applying the paragraph 32 presumption that previously developed sites should be developed before greenfield sites, but it is not a trumping factor that automatically permits greenfield release wherever brownfield capacity remains.
legal_issues: Whether PPG3 paragraph 32 requires refusal of greenfield housing unless no brownfield site remains
How paragraph 34's five-year housing supply guidance relates to paragraph 32 at appeal stage
Whether the Secretary of State's decision was flawed for lack of reasons

confidence.notes: Outcome, PPG3 analysis, and remittal order are explicit. PPG3 is government guidance rather than statute; no linked cases are cited by name in the available text.

enrichment.short_title: DPP challenge to magistrates' s20 sentencing jurisdiction
key_facts: An 18-year-old schoolboy pleaded guilty under Plea Before Venue to inflicting grievous bodily harm after a drunken assault at a school party.
The victim's spleen was removed and he required lifelong medication, but the justices accepted jurisdiction rather than committing the case to the Crown Court.
The DPP sought judicial review, arguing the facts were so grave that retention of jurisdiction was irrational or truly astonishing.
The application was brought about ten weeks after the jurisdiction decision and while the defendant remained unsentenced.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review, heard in the Administrative Court with permission granted on paper.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused on merits and for lack of promptness.
enrichment.ratio: A challenge to magistrates' decision to retain jurisdiction for sentencing after a guilty plea under Plea Before Venue succeeds only if the decision was truly astonishing or perverse; delay in bringing judicial review, especially where a young defendant remains unsentenced, may itself justify refusal of relief.
legal_issues: Whether the justices' acceptance of jurisdiction for a section 20 offence was truly astonishing
Whether the DPP acted promptly enough in seeking judicial review
Application of national mode of trial guidelines for section 20 offences
linked_authorities: R v Acton Crown Court, ex parte Bewley
Director of Public Prosecutions v Salisbury Justices

confidence.notes: Facts, statutory framework, test, and dismissal are clearly stated. Judge metadata in the source file is empty.

enrichment.short_title: Statutory demand and arbitration stay in building dispute

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: A homeowner disputed interim payment certificates under a JCT intermediate building contract for works at 98 Hamilton Terrace.
The contractor served two statutory demands totalling over £133,000 based on architect's certificates.
The debtor applied to set aside the demands, arguing an arbitration clause meant the demands should be set aside and that cross-claims exceeded the debts.
The Chief Registrar found cross-claims fell short by £62,348.16 and rejected the arbitration-based challenge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court (Chancery Division) against orders dismissing applications to set aside statutory demands.
enrichment.ratio: Service of a statutory demand is not a legal proceeding for the purposes of section 9 of the Arbitration Act 1996; a creditor may pursue bankruptcy proceedings despite an arbitration agreement unless rule 6.5(4)(d) grounds show it would be unjust for the demand to stand, and a mere possibility of a later stay is insufficient where no arbitration had been commenced.
legal_issues: Whether service of a statutory demand constitutes legal proceedings under section 9 Arbitration Act 1996
Whether a future bankruptcy petition bound to be stayed justifies setting aside a demand under rule 6.5(4)(d)
Whether cross-claims equalled or exceeded the debts claimed
index_terms: Halki Shipping Corporation v Sopex Oils Ltd
Royal Bank of Scotland v Binnell
linked_authorities: Halki Shipping Corporation v Sopex Oils Ltd
In re A Debtor (Nos 49 and 50 of 1992)
Royal Bank of Scotland v Binnell

enrichment.short_title: Co-accused bad character in cutthroat manslaughter trial
key_facts: Randall was convicted of manslaughter after trial for murder following fatal head injuries to Michael Barber near Rickmansworth.
In a cutthroat defence, Randall said Glean inflicted the fatal blows; Glean denied involvement outside the house.
The trial judge directed that Glean's violent record was relevant only to his credibility, not to who was more likely to have killed Barber.
Randall had admitted kicking Barber once but denied causing the multiple fatal injuries.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the bad-character direction ground and a retrial ordered; second ground dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: In an unusual cutthroat case, a co-accused's antecedent history of serious violence may be relevant not only to credibility but also to whether one defendant's account is more probable than the other's, following Lowery and Thompson; limiting the jury to credibility-only use was a significant misdirection.
legal_issues: Admissibility and use of a co-accused's bad character in a cutthroat defence
Whether the manslaughter direction was adequate despite a late comprehensive direction

confidence.notes: Grounds, authorities, and retrial order are clearly set out in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: University copyright in Simcyp drug simulation software
key_facts: Sheffield University developed pharmacokinetic research software (Simcyp) to predict drug-body interactions.
Under a research agreement, Cyprotex programmer Dr Edwards converted the project into a marketable Java-based program.
The parties disputed whether copyright in the Java program belonged to Sheffield as resulting IP or to Cyprotex as sponsor IP under clause 9.
Sheffield had licensed Cyprotex for internal research use but sought ownership to commercialise the program.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Technology and Construction Court on copyright ownership and related relief.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; declaration that copyright in Simcyp, MathCAD, related algorithms, databases, and specifications is owned by the University of Sheffield, with assignment and delivery-up orders to follow.
enrichment.ratio: On the facts, Java programming work was either resulting intellectual property jointly created by Sheffield and sponsor employees under the research agreement, or alternatively a term should be implied that copyright vested in Sheffield where the purpose was to transform the university's research into a commercially marketable program while the sponsor retained only an internal-use licence.
legal_issues: Construction of intellectual property clauses in a university research sponsorship agreement
Ownership of copyright in software developed from academic research by a sponsor's employee
Whether an implied term assigns copyright to the commissioning university
linked_authorities: Nichols Advanced Vehicle Systems Inc v Rees

confidence.notes: Detailed contract and copyright analysis with clear declaratory relief. Judgment is lengthy but the dispositive reasoning is explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentences for Pit Bull Crew gang
key_facts: Nine members of the Manchester Pit Bull Crew gang were convicted of conspiracies to possess firearms with intent to endanger life and to supply Class A and B drugs.
The gang operated a large-scale drug business protected by loaded firearms, balaclavas, body armour, and territorial violence from 1999 to 2000.
Original sentences ranged from four-and-a-half to nine years depending on seniority and role.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient for senior members; junior members' sentences were left intact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference for unduly lenient sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Reference granted; senior members Gordon, Thorne, Boakye, and Simons received increased total sentences of ten to twelve years on resentencing; junior members' sentences stood.
enrichment.ratio: In a large-scale armed drug-gang conspiracy where firearms were integral to the business, starting points for senior participants should have been substantially higher, with consecutive or adjusted concurrent terms reflecting both firearms and drugs conspiracies; youth and lesser involvement may justify leaving junior members' lenient sentences undisturbed.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentencing levels for conspiracy to possess firearms with intent to endanger life
Sentencing for large-scale Class A drug conspiracy combined with gang firearms use
Distinction between senior and junior gang members on an Attorney General's reference

confidence.notes: Sentencing outcomes for each offender category are clearly recorded. Specific statutory provisions for the conspiracy counts are not quoted verbatim.

enrichment.short_title: Gurkha veterans' pension and family service challenge
key_facts: Seven retired Gurkha soldiers resident in Nepal challenged MoD terms as discriminatory compared with British Army soldiers.
Gurkhas are Nepalese citizens who serve under special tripartite arrangements dating from 1947, with Indian Army-linked pay and pensions.
The claimants pursued pensions and accompanied-service complaints; other alleged discrimination points were abandoned or narrowed.
Gurkha pensions are tailored to Nepalese cost of living and are substantially higher than local professional salaries.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim in the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Claims dismissed; pension arrangements upheld as lawful and proportionate; no declaratory relief granted on accompanied service for these retired claimants.
enrichment.ratio: Different pension arrangements for Gurkhas lawfully reflect nationality and retirement in Nepal rather than race, and are not disproportionate where tailored to Nepalese conditions; a 25% cap on accompanied service cannot be justified by the 1947 tripartite agreement alone, but retired claimants were not entitled to the broad declaratory relief sought.
legal_issues: Whether Gurkha pension differences breach Article 14 read with Protocol 1 Article 1
Whether discrimination is on grounds of race or nationality
Whether the 25% accompanied-service limit breaches Article 8 read with Article 14
linked_authorities: Wandsworth London Borough Council v Michalak
R (Carson) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions

confidence.notes: Detailed Michalak analysis on both pensions and accompanied service. Many cited authorities were not individually analysed in the judgment text.

enrichment.short_title: Enforcing Building Act demolition notice after delay
key_facts: An unauthorised rear extension at 46 New Cross Road was built in 1988 without planning or building approvals.
A section 36 demolition notice was served in 1988; appeal and earlier judicial review failed, but demolition was not carried out until 2000.
The extension was later used as a church, generating neighbour noise complaints and an ombudsman complaint about council inaction.
In April 2000 Lewisham resolved to enforce the notice twelve years after it was served.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of judicial review of the council's decision to enforce a section 36 notice.
enrichment.ratio: Long delay in enforcing a valid section 36 demolition notice does not automatically bar enforcement where the purpose remains the same and the owner has suffered no specific prejudice from the delay; a council may legitimately consider neighbour hardship and public reaction when deciding when to activate enforcement.
legal_issues: Whether a section 36 notice becomes unenforceable after prolonged delay
Whether enforcement was motivated by improper purpose rather than Building Act duties
Applicability of Grice v Dudley Corporation to demolition notices

confidence.notes: Limited grounds on appeal and outcome are clearly explained. Planning Act history is background only.

enrichment.short_title: Time-limited farm repurchase option and perpetuities
key_facts: Cross Roads Farm was sold by the Trueloves' company to the Wilson family in 1974 for £20,000 under a written agreement.
The agreement gave the Trueloves an unlimited right to repurchase the farm for £20,000 on specified death events.
Mr Wilson died in 1981; Mrs Wilson and David Wilson remained owners and resisted repurchase.
Both sides had solicitors in 1974 but neither appreciated the option would void under the rule against perpetuities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Chancery Division on validity of a contractual repurchase option.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants succeeded; repurchase option void under section 9(2); no rectification or estoppel; land charge registration vacated.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual right to repurchase land granted in 1974 without a time limit was an option to acquire an interest in land that vested immediately and became void under section 9(2) of the Perpetuities and Accumulations Act 1964; mutual mistake as to perpetuity rules does not justify rectification or estoppel where neither party represented that statutory rights would not be relied upon.
legal_issues: When an option to repurchase land vests for perpetuity purposes
Whether rectification can rewrite an unlimited option into a valid term
Whether estoppel or equity prevents reliance on section 9(2)
index_terms: London & South Western Railway Co v Gomm
linked_authorities: London & South Western Railway Co v Gomm

confidence.notes: Three issues and orders are clearly resolved. Source judge metadata incorrectly lists Lord Denning MR.

enrichment.short_title: Garden dwelling refused as countryside development
key_facts: Mr Hayter applied for permission to build a four-bedroom house in the garden of Beeches Hill, Bishop's Waltham.
Winchester Council refused permission because the site lay outside the local plan inset and was countryside development contrary to structure and local plan policies.
The claimant argued the site fell within an H2 development frontage and that PPG3 favoured previously developed land.
An inspector dismissed the appeal, finding a distinct change in development pattern at the junction and harm to countryside character.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to a planning inspector's appeal decision, heard by Collins J.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge dismissed; inspector's decision upheld; costs assessed at £3,679.25.
enrichment.ratio: Where a proposal site lies outside the local plan inset boundary, policy H2 development frontages do not apply and countryside policies govern; PPG3 does not override those restrictions to permit backland garden development, and the inspector's planning judgment on character and appearance is not reviewable as an error of law.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal site was within the Beeches Hill development frontage or countryside
Whether PPG3 previously developed land policy superseded local plan countryside restrictions
Whether the inspector misidentified the main issue or prejudged the appeal

confidence.notes: Planning policy analysis and dismissal are clear. PPG3 and PPG12 are guidance rather than statute; no case authorities are cited.
